newsitem.title: USA: BPA sees Pacific Intertie line at 3,600 MW by Dec.
newsitem.headline: BPA sees Pacific Intertie line at 3,600 MW by Dec.

text.p: Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) expects capacity on the AC segment of the Pacific Intertie to increase to 3,600 megawatts (MW) within the next 30 days, BPA administrator Randy Hardy said Thursday.

The line, part of the high-voltage system linking Northwest hydroelectric plants to the California power market, has been capped at 3,200 MW, well below its 4,800 MW capacity, since a major power outage hit the western grid August 10.
Hardy, speaking here at a Congressional subcommitteee hearing on the outage, said work to correct voltage support problems at the McNary hydroelectric dam on the Columbia River are almost finished.
Voltage problems at McNary were a central factor in the blackout, which hit several states.

Hardy also said BPA hopes to be able to raise the load on the AC line to above 4,000 MW by April, 1997, in time for the spring runoff, when water levels and power generation typically hit their seasonal peak.
But that schedule will depend on completion of a system-wide voltage support study. The study is expected to be submitted by January 1.

"An exact time frame depends on the degree of changes (recommended by the study) as well as equipment needs," he said, adding that some key equipment needed to upgrade the system already had been ordered.

He noted that some additional capacity could be added to the DC segment of the Intertie, which is currently limited to around 2,000 MW of its 3,200 MW capacity, depending on what is agreed by members of the Western System Coordinating Council (WSCC).
WSCC is the industry group that oversees operation of the western power grid.
BPA is a federal agency based in Portland, Ore., in charge of marketing electricty from U.S. hydroelectric projects in the Northwest, mostly on the Columbia and Snake Rivers.
